1.translation: Then, when [Dhṛtarāṣṭra] was awaiting the answer to “What happened?”, Sañjaya said: “Him in that condition”—him whose eyes were full and agitated with tears. To Arjuna, grieving in the manner just described, Madhusūdana spoke these words.

2.translation: He states that very speech: “Why?”—for what reason? “You” means you. In this crisis, this confusion and delusion has arisen and come upon you, although it is not resorted to by the noble, does not lead to heaven, is unrighteous, and brings infamy.
word_for_word: in a crisis; in a difficult situation
because it is not resorted to by the noble

3.translation: Therefore, [he says] with “cowardice”: O Pārtha, do not yield to cowardice—do not enter into it—for this does not befit you. Abandoning this petty weakness of heart, this cowardice, rise for battle, O scorcher of enemies.

because this is not fitting for you

4.translation: Arjuna said: I have not withdrawn from [battle] through cowardice, but because this battle is unjust. How shall I fight Bhīṣma and Droṇa, who are worthy of worship? In that case, even with arrows? Where it would be improper even to say with words, “I shall fight,” how could I fight with arrows? O slayer of enemies.

5.translation: If it is said, “Then your bodily maintenance would not even occur,” he answers with “the gurus.” Having killed Droṇa and the other gurus, the killing of a guru being opposed to the next world, it is better—proper—even in this world to eat alms-food without doing that. On the other hand, by killing the gurus I would experience here itself the suffering of hell: I would eat and enjoy pleasures consisting of wealth and desire, thoroughly smeared with their blood. Alternatively, “wealth and desire” qualifies the gurus: being agitated by thirst for wealth, they would not withdraw from battle, so their killing would necessarily follow. Thus Bhīṣma said to Yudhiṣṭhira: “A man is the servant of wealth; wealth is the servant of no one. This is true, great king: I am bound to the Kauravas by wealth.”

We do not know which of the two would be greater: whether we should conquer them or they should conquer us. 7.translation: With “by faintheartedness”: my nature, marked by courage and the like, has been overwhelmed by the defect of faintheartedness—the fault produced by the destruction of my own family—and by that fault. “How shall we live after killing these?” I am overcome by those two. My mind is also confused about dharma: I am doubtful whether, for a kṣatriya, begging after abandoning battle is dharma or adharma. Therefore, tell me what you determine to be truly beneficial and fitting. Moreover, I am your disciple, worthy of instruction; therefore teach me, who have taken refuge in you.

8.translation: If you say, “You yourself should consider what is fitting and then do it,” he answers, “No.” I do not see any action that could remove my grief—the grief that dries up the senses. Even if I were to obtain an unconquered and prosperous kingdom on earth, or even lordship over the gods, I do not see a means of removing grief. The meaning is that, even after obtaining every desired thing, I still do not see a way to dispel my sorrow.

11.translation: Because grief arises from failing to distinguish the body from the Self, the Blessed Lord says “you grieve for those who are not to be grieved,” in order to teach that distinction. You grieve for relatives who are not objects of grief, having grieved after seeing your own people assembled and ready to fight, as in “Seeing these relatives standing before me, O Kṛṣṇa, desiring to fight,” and so on. Although I instructed you with “Why has this confusion come upon you in this crisis?”, you merely utter the words of the learned—“How shall I fight Bhīṣma in battle?” and the like; you are not learned. For the wise do not grieve for relatives who have lost their lives, nor for those who are still alive, thinking, “How will these live, even though bereft of their relatives?”

12.translation: He gives the reason for their not being objects of grief with “never indeed.” Just as I, the Supreme Lord, was never non-existent—not at any time—even when the manifestation and withdrawal of my sport-body occurred, but always existed because I am beginningless, so you too were never non-existent; you always existed. These rulers also were never non-existent; they always existed, being portions of Me. Nor will we hereafter become non-existent; we will continue to exist. The meaning is that they are not to be grieved for because they are free from birth and death.

13.translation: One may object: “It is certainly true that you, the Lord, are free from birth and death; but birth and death are well known in the case of living beings.” He answers with “for the embodied.” For the embodied one, the living being identified with the body, childhood and the other stages in this gross body are dependent on the body, not on the Self. Even when a former stage has ended and another has arisen, the very same “I” is recognized. In the same way, when this body is destroyed, the attainment of another body also depends on the subtle body; the Self is not destroyed. We see a newborn immediately inclined toward suckling and the like because of previous impressions. Therefore the steadfast person, the intelligent one, is not deluded by the destruction and arising of those two bodies; he does not think, “the Self itself has died or been born.”

14.translation: One may say: “I do not grieve for the dead or the living; I grieve only for myself, who experiences the suffering of separation and the like.” He answers with “the contacts of the sense-measures.” The sense-functions are called “measures” because objects are measured or known through them; their contacts with objects produce cold, heat, and the like. Since they are transient—subject to coming and going and therefore unstable—endure them. Just as contact with water, sunlight, and the like produces cold, heat, and the like at particular times, according to their nature, so union with and separation from what is desired produce pleasure, pain, and the like. Since these too are unstable, endurance is proper for you, who are steadfast; you should not become subject to the joy and grief caused by them.

15.translation: It is even more proper to endure them than to strive to remedy them, because endurance bears great fruit. He says “the person whom”: these contacts of the sense-measures do not afflict or overpower the person whom they do not disturb, and whose pleasure and pain are equal. Such a person, not being agitated by them, becomes fit for immortality—liberation—through the means of dharma and knowledge.

16.translation: One may object: “Even so, how can unbearably intense heat, cold, and the like be endured? And if they are endured completely, the body itself might sometimes be destroyed.” With the intention that everything can be endured through inquiry into reality, he says “the unreal.” Heat, cold, and the like, being unreal because they are not properties of the Self, have no existence in the Self. Likewise, the existent—the Self whose nature is being—has no non-existence or destruction. Thus the conclusion concerning both the existent and the non-existent has been seen by those who see reality, who know a thing as it truly is. The meaning is: endure them together with this discrimination.

17.translation: There the imperishable reality, whose nature is being, was stated generally; he presents it specifically with “imperishable.” Know that which, as the witness, pervades all this—everything extended from the body onward and subject to coming and going. That, whose nature is the Self, is imperishable, free from destruction. He gives the reason with “that which is subject to destruction.”

18.translation: He presents the body as subject to coming and going with “having an end.” Those in which an end, destruction, is present are “having an end.” These bodies, which possess pleasure, pain, and the other changing properties, are said by those who see reality to belong to the embodied one—the possessor of a body—who is eternal, always of one nature, therefore imperishable, and immeasurable, not limited by anything. Since the Self is not destroyed and has no relation to pleasure, pain, and the like, abandon the sorrow born of delusion and fight. The meaning is: do not abandon your own dharma.

19.translation: Thus the sorrow caused by the death of Bhīṣma and the others has been removed. The distress attributed to the Self as the killer, expressed in “I do not wish to kill these,” is likewise without a basis. “This” means the Self. The meaning is that the Self is neither an object in the act of killing nor its agent; the reason is given by “this is not [born or slain].”

20.translation: He strengthens the statement “it is not slain” by showing that the Self is free from the six modifications of existence. “It is not born” denies birth; “nor does it die” denies destruction. The two uses of “and” have an emphatic sense. Nor, having come into being, does it later become existent: this denies the second modification, existence after birth. The reason is that it is unborn. Whatever is born comes to exist after birth, but what exists by itself does not acquire another existence. “Eternal” denies growth, since it is always of one nature. “Everlasting” denies decline, since it is continually existent. “Ancient” denies transformation: it was already ancient, yet ever new, and does not become new by changing into another form. Alternatively, taking “does not become” along with what follows, it denies increase— it does not become greater or more than it is. “Unborn” and “eternal” give the reason why neither kind of increase occurs, so there is no repetition. Thus the six modifications taught by Yāska and other Vedic authorities—being born, existing, growing, transforming, declining, and perishing—are all rejected. He concludes the intended absence of destruction with “it is not slain when the body is slain.”

21.translation: For this very reason, the absence of agency as killer, stated earlier, is also established; he says “he who knows.” Whoever knows the Self as eternal, free from growth, undecaying, unborn, and imperishable—whom does that person kill, and how? There is no means for killing such a one. And having himself become the instigator, whom could he cause another to kill? The meaning is: no one, in any way. By this it is also said, “Do not see fault in Me because I am the instigator as well.”

24.translation: He gives the reasons for this in the next verse and a half: because the Self has no parts, it cannot be cut or wetted. Because it is formless, it cannot be burned; because it has no fluidity, it cannot be dried. Therefore it is not capable of being cut and the like. It is eternal, imperishable, all-pervading, immovable, of stable nature, free from acquiring another form, unchanging because it does not abandon its former form, and beginningless.

25.translation: Moreover, the Self is unmanifest—it is not an object of the eyes and the other senses; inconceivable—it is not even an object of the mind; and immutable—it is not accessible to the organs of action. With “it is said,” he establishes the authority of statements by experts concerning its eternality and the like. He concludes with “therefore.”

26.translation: Thus it was said that there should be no grief because the Self has no birth or destruction. Now, even if one accepts that the Self is born together with the body and destroyed when that body is destroyed, he says that grief is still not proper. Even if you think that this Self is eternal—always born whenever each particular body is born, and dead whenever that body dies, because birth and death, the results of good and bad karma, belong to the Self—you still ought not to grieve.

27.translation: He explains why with “for one who is born.” For one who has been born, death is certainly inevitable when the karma that began this life is exhausted; and for one who has died, birth is certainly inevitable through the karma that produces the next body. Therefore, in a matter that cannot be avoided—a matter whose nature is birth and death—you, who are learned, ought not to grieve; you are not fit to do so.

28.translation: Moreover, after considering the nature of the bodies and the birth and death of the Self only as conditioned by those limiting adjuncts, he says that grief is not proper with “unmanifest in the beginning.” The primordial cause is unmanifest; therefore these bodies are “unmanifest in the beginning,” since even while remaining in causal form they arise only later. They are manifest in the middle—their state between birth and death—and they are unmanifest at the end, dissolving back into that condition. For beings of this nature, what occasion is there for lamentation, and what reason is there for sorrow and wailing? The meaning is that grief is no more fitting than grief over objects seen in a dream after one has awakened.

29.translation: Why, then, do even learned people in the world grieve? With the intention that they do so only because of ignorance of the Self, he teaches that the Self is difficult to know with “as a wonder.” Someone sees this Self through the teaching of scripture and teacher, and sees it as a wonder. Because the Self is beyond ordinary experience, of the nature of all-pervading eternal knowledge and bliss, he looks upon it with amazement, as though seeing something impossible, being overwhelmed by the thought that it could not be so. Another speaks of it with wonder, and another hears of it with wonder. Yet another, overwhelmed by a contrary conception, does not truly know it even after hearing; and, by the force of the “and,” one should understand that even after explaining it, he does not know it correctly.

31.translation: What Arjuna said—“trembling arises in my body”—is also improper, he says with “your own dharma.” Because the Self is not destroyed, you ought not to tremble even at the killing of these people. Moreover, the sentence is connected with “even after considering your own dharma”: having considered your own dharma as well, you ought not to tremble. To what Arjuna said—“I see no good in killing my own people in battle” and the like—he answers with “than a righteous battle”: for a kṣatriya there is nothing higher than a battle that is just and does not depart from dharma.

38.translation: To what was also said—“sin alone would take hold of us”—he answers with “pleasure and pain.” Make pleasure and pain equal, and likewise make gain and loss equal, and victory and defeat, which are causes of those two, equal as well. 39.translation: Having concluded the knowledge-yoga that was taught, he introduces karma-yoga, its means, with “this has been told to you.” Through it reality is correctly made known; therefore “sāṅkhya” means right knowledge, and the understanding that reveals the Self’s reality within that knowledge is the understanding to be cultivated. Even if, despite this understanding of Sāṅkhya having been taught, direct knowledge of the Self does not arise for you, then hear this understanding concerning karma-yoga, by which direct knowledge of the Self arises through purification of the inner instrument. Joined to this understanding and purified through karma-yoga offered to the Supreme Lord, you will thoroughly cast off the bondage made of karma through direct knowledge obtained by His grace.

40.translation: One may object: “In actions such as agriculture, the result may fail because of many obstacles, and a ritual defect in a mantra or other limb may produce an adverse result. 41.translation: Anticipating the question “why?”, he states the difference between the two with “resolute.” Here, in karma-yoga characterized by worship of the Lord, there is a single, one-pointed understanding, resolute because it is certain: “Through devotion to the Supreme Lord I will certainly cross over.” But for those who lack such resolution—those of many aims and full of desires—understandings are many and branched in countless directions, because their desires are countless and because karma, its qualities, and its fruits differ. The daily and occasional duties performed for worship of the Lord do not perish even through a small defect in a limb; they are prescribed with the instruction, “Let him do them as he is able.” Nor is there a defect, because the stopping of a defect occurs through their being directed to the Lord. Desire-motivated action is different: “Let him offer the Agnihotra for one who desires heaven”; “let him offer with curds for one who desires the sense-world.” This is the great difference.

42.translation: One may object: “Why do even those who desire results not abandon difficult desires and cultivate the resolute understanding alone?” He answers with “the words they speak.” Those who speak flowery words—excellent at first hearing, like a flowering poisonous creeper, and directed only toward results such as heaven—have their minds carried away by those words; for them no resolute understanding is established. Why do they speak in this way? Because they are undiscerning and deluded. The reason is that they delight only in the Vedic statements of praise, such as “the merit of one who performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifice becomes imperishable” and “we have become immortal by drinking Soma.” Therefore they habitually say that there is no higher reality to be attained beyond this.

45.translation: One may object: “If heaven and the like are not the highest result, why do the Vedas prescribe actions as the means to them?” He answers with “whose subject is the three guṇas.” The Vedas, which explain the connection between ritual actions and their fruits, concern those qualified persons who are composed of the three guṇas and who desire results. But you should be beyond the three guṇas; become free from desire. He explains the means: be free from duality—the pairs such as pleasure and pain, heat and cold—and endure them. He says how: remain established in the ever-present sattva; that is, rely on courage. Likewise be free from yoga and kṣema: yoga is accepting what has not been obtained, and kṣema is preserving what has been obtained. Be free from both and remain vigilant, not careless. One agitated by duality and occupied with acquisition and preservation cannot transcend the three guṇas.

46.translation: One may object: “The resolute understanding concerned with worshipping the Lord without desire, abandoning the many results taught by the Veda, is surely a wrong understanding.” He answers with “as much as.” A small reservoir—a well, pond, or tank—is a place where water is drunk; because it contains only a small amount of water in one location, one moves around it to obtain separately whatever use is needed, such as bathing or drinking. But in a great lake with water overflowing everywhere, all those uses are found in one place. In the same way, whatever value exists throughout all the Vedas in the form of particular actions and their fruits is found entirely in the Brāhmaṇa who knows reality and is established in Brahman. Lesser joys are included in the bliss of Brahman, as the scripture says, “Other beings live by a measure of this very bliss.” Therefore this understanding alone is right understanding.

47.translation: One may object: “Then, intending that all the fruits of action will arise simply through worship of the Supreme Lord, should one act? Why act at all?” He prevents this with “your entitlement is only to action.” You, who seek knowledge of reality, have entitlement only to action; there should be no desire for its fruits, which are causes of bondage. One may object: “When action is performed, its fruit must arise, just as satisfaction follows eating.” He answers: do not become one whose action is motivated by its fruit; do not make the fruit of action the cause of your activity. Only the desired heaven and the like, specified as the fruit for the person enjoined to act, are the fruit; an undesired fruit does not arise. Therefore, from fear that the fruit will become binding, do not become attached to inaction either; do not make non-performance of action your commitment.

59.translation: One may object: “The absence of engagement with sense-objects cannot be the mark of a person of steady wisdom, since the inert, the sick, and those devoted to fasting likewise do not engage with objects.” He answers with “the objects.” The senses’ taking in of objects is called their “eating” or receiving them. For an ignorant person identified with the body, who is without this food and does not take in objects through the senses, the objects withdraw; that is, the experience of them ceases. But the taste—attachment, desire—remains; the desire does not cease. For this person of steady wisdom, however, even the taste, the attachment, naturally withdraws on seeing the Supreme Self; it is destroyed. Alternatively, for one without food, devoted to fasting, objects generally withdraw because one tormented by hunger has no expectation of sound, touch, and the rest. But the taste alone remains; the expectation of taste does not cease. The remainder has the same meaning.
